#8000. I Travel With A Kid Who Has Severe Allergies. Here Are The Things I Never Thought To Worry About

Everyday things can send us to the hospital. Now I’m prepared and am sharing the wealth.

My son has severe allergies, asthma, and celiac disease, so everyday things can sometimes send us to the hospital. And traveling adds another layer of uncertainty. A hotel room that looks clean could be holding fragrances that trigger respiratory symptoms. The swimming pool down the hall could pose problemsThat gluten-free item on the menu during our family night out could be cross-contaminated. As a parent, I’ve learned that keeping my son safe means thinking beyond the obvious risks.

With the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane. So, I chatted with experts Dr. Sarah Beebe, a travel advisor and autism travel professional based in Lewes, Delaware, and Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician with 20 years experience in urgent care, who helped me identify the less obvious triggers families might encounter while traveling—and how to better prepare for them.

Through the colder months and when planning trips, I’d always assumed that keeping my son’s inhaler on hand was enough. But a recent hospital stay made me realize his asthma is far more severe than we’d understood, and that I needed to take a more proactive approach to managing it.

I researched all of the common triggers, such as dust, pet dander, pollen, smoke and weather changes. After chatting with Dr. Tyson and Dr. Beebe, I learned of the lesser-known hazards that can lurk in the places we stay and the ways we travel.

“A lot of high-end hotels have a signature scent in the lobby and common areas, and most people find it lovely, but for a kid with asthma or sensory sensitivities, it can be a lot,” Beebe told me. No parent can demand these scents be removed, of course. But we can be aware and prepare accordingly.

On top of fragrances, “detergents in bedding and cleaning supplies will do it, too,” Tyson said. What can families do? Request fragrance-free bedding, or bring their own.

When planning family trips, we always look for a place with a pool. Swimming is one of our favorite pastimes, and I never considered that it might be contributing to my kids’ symptoms. But thinking back, my son often develops a runny nose and needs to lie down after a swim.

“The heavy chlorine smell is actually chloramines sitting in the air over a pool that isn't well ventilated, and it's a real irritant,” Beebe explained. She once treated a child who came into the emergency room she was working in after swimming multiple days in a hotel pool. “He began having a cough and shortness of breath. He came to the ER in significant distress because the high levels of chlorine in the pool triggered a more severe asthma exacerbation and he didn’t have any rescue medications with him,” she said. Luckily, there was an emergency room nearby.

“Thunderstorms can break up pollen and trigger asthma,” Tyson explained. When traveling through the rainy season, keep windows closed and stay indoors when storms approach. But don’t assume the risk disappears as soon as the skies clear; thunderstorm-related asthma can occur after the storm. If you do venture outside, have your child rinse off and change clothes when you return to your lodging, to help remove pollen from the skin and hair.

Planning a New Year’s trip with the kids? Keep in mind that fireworks can pose a double challenge for autistic kids with asthma. “Fireworks smoke blows right over the crowd depending on the wind,” Beebe shared, and the noise and crowds can add another layer of sensory overwhelm. Her advice? Find a viewing spot farther from the launch site and upwind of the smoke, if possible. Your child can enjoy the show without being right in the middle of it.

Along with his many allergies, my son has severe celiac disease. When his symptoms first appeared, doctors were concerned enough that they thought his presentation resembled leukemia. He was spiking fevers, developing spots on his skin, struggling with abdominal issues and shortness of breath. My son would wake up fine, then spike a fever by noon and be on the couch until dinner—for days and days until we figured it out.

Now, when he’s exposed to gluten, he can vomit profusely. And for him, the risk isn’t limited to taking a bite of food containing gluten. Cross-contact –when gluten transfers from contaminated surfaces or other foods — can be a problem, too.

And so I chatted with Tyson and Beebe about what celiac triggers to look for when not at home.

“Welcome treats, lounge snacks, the chocolate on the pillow. None of it gets the care a restaurant meal does,” Beebe said. “And half the time it isn't gluten-free, never mind certified.” If your child is young, there’s a chance they may snag one or more of these things when your back is turned, so we have to think ahead. “When I plan a trip, I have the allergy flagged on the reservation so the extras get caught too, not just the dining rooms,” Beebe added.

Paper straws had never crossed my mind as a potential source of gluten exposure. I can think of more than one time I’ve bought my son a drink without giving the straw a second thought. “A lot of them use a wheat-based binder to hold the straw together,” Beebe said. “So even the eco-friendly straw can be a problem.” Keeping a few reusable or plastic straws on hand–or bringing your own drinks—can offer a simple alternative.

Traveling in different countries is ever harder, since the warnings aren’t as clear and there is often unintended gluten exposure, Tyson told me. “This is the one families never see coming, and it's the one I warn them about,” Beebe said. “You’re fine early in the trip, but after days of eating where you can't control the kitchen, the little exposures stack up, and the worst reaction tends to hit at the very end.”

One thing Tyson pointed out that I hadn’t considered is how the stress of travel can complicate celiac disease management. Even without a known gluten exposure, the disruption of routines can affect how your child feels. “During travel people often allow little amounts of gluten which combined with above can cause a flare,” she said.

So, what can families do to help with all of this? Well, plan travel around places known as safe havens for people with celiac disease. Disney has an entire department devoted to complex allergies, Beebe shared. “And you can call ahead of time, so they're prepared for your kids with severe and complex needs before you ever arrive.”

Learning about these lesser known triggers has given me something I didn’t have before: a greater sense of control. Instead of approaching travel with the anxiety and dread that can come with managing my kids’ needs away from home, I feel more equipped to protect him–and more excited about the adventures ahead.

This holiday season, as we move from one place to the next, we’ll be better prepared for what we might encounter along the way. And if you’re coparenting like I am, there’s another kind of peace that comes with this knowledge: knowing you can share what you’ve learned with the people caring for your children, so they can help keep them safe, too. We may not be able to anticipate every trigger, but we can make it easier for our kids to explore the world with a little less risk–and a lot less worry.

#7999. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

This time of year may see reduced raised bed activity, but these quick tasks can prep your beds for the cold months ahead and ensure better productivity when spring returns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

Galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

For healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

Intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

Spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

Inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

If your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

For tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

#7996. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#7995. The KJH Microscara Has The Tiniest Wand Ever & That's Why It's Perfect

Fuller looking lashes with zero transfer? Yes please.

As a fair-skinned, dark-haired lady of Scottish descent, I haven’t always appreciated my very hairy ancestry (like when my little brother told me I have arms hairier than a man’s). But along with the body hair gene comes one I’m thankful for: I’ve always had long eyelashes. When I’m shopping for mascaras, I gravitate toward volumizing formulas that make my lashes look full from root to tip. And as I get older and the skin around my eyes creases and (sob) sags in new ways, I also need mascaras that won’t transfer and leave dark smudges on my top and bottom lids.

When KJH — a brand founded by celebrity MUA Katie Jane Hughes — offered to send me their new Microscara, I was intrigued. I love a tubing mascara because they’re pretty darn transfer proof (and the easy removal is so nice), but I wasn’t sure how volumizing a tubing formula could really be. And that teensy wand? I dunno... But let me tell you, after wearing it for months, this is the stuff right here.

KJH describes the Microscara as a smudge-proof tubing mascara that “delivers instant volume and length that lasts.” The differentiator here is the micro wand designed to grab and coat even the smallest, hardest-to-reach lashes for a “full-lash finish that won’t budge.”

The Microscara’s big selling point is the small wand. It’s about half the length of your typical mascara wand, and it is very slim at the tapered end. The bristles feel like a typical volumizing wand (more, thinner bristles instead of the spiky plastic kind). And because the brush is so slim, the tube is too — it’s extremely lightweight and lovely to travel with.

Mascara is always the last step in my makeup routine (even after setting spray, because I don’t want to wet my mascara and encourage smudging). With any mascara, I like to hold the brush right at the root of my lashes, wiggle it back and forth so the bristles can grab on, and then move the wand up to coat each lash. My best tip is to also hold the wand behind your lashes to coat the tops and catch the curly tips of each eyelash. You’ll be shocked how much visual length this adds to your lashes overall.

My whole routine works so much better with the Microscara because of its slim brush. I’m not accidentally getting mascara on my lids, and I can wiggle the brush into the corners of my eyes and coat even the smallest lashes.

A little side-by-side comparison of my bare lashes and the KJH Microscara’s handiwork.

OK, one of my favorite things about using the KJH Microscara is that, because I can get so close to my lash line with the little brush, it basically looks like I’m wearing eyeliner and can skip that step completely. My lash line itself just looks fuller. C’est magnifique.

With other tubing formulas, I feel like they add length but my lashes end up looking a little sparse, and that is simply not the case here. I can see a genuine difference in the look of both the volume and length of my lashes when I use the product. I am someone who gets mascara smudges with pretty much any formula (even the waterproof ones), but this product has only ever given me a smudge once, and I think it was my fault, TBH.

Much like foundations, mascaras can be pretty personal. What works like a dream for one person could be a disaster on someone else. But I think if you’re in the market for a mascara that adds volume and is easy to remove, you won’t be disappointed by the Microscara.

I haven’t reached for any other mascara since I cracked the lid on this one.

#7994. Actress Chloe Bridges and Dr. Charis Chambers on what moms need to know to help protect their baby against RSV infection

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 25, 2026

This article is sponsored by Pfizer. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

This episode is sponsored by Pfizer. This article is directed to a U.S. audience and may not be suitable for those outside of the U.S. We partnered with them to bring you this conversation, but everything you hear from me, Chloe, and Dr. Chambers is our own experience and opinion. Not medical advice, just a conversation between moms.

Pregnancy has a way of making you feel responsible for someone before you have ever met them. For actress Chloe Bridges and OBGYN Dr. Charis Chambers, that meant navigating the identity shift of new motherhood while also learning about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a highly contagious respiratory virus that is the number one cause of hospitalization for babies in the United States with nearly 50% of RSV hospitalizations occurring during the first 3 months of life. Both moms built a trusted village of support to help navigate – and have a lot to say about what they wish they had known sooner.

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

Chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

Dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. She is the Chief Medical Officer at the cycle-tracking app Clue and the author of The Period and Puberty Parenting Revolution. She lives with her husband, Zachary, and their son, Joshua.

Chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. I’d be like, ‘Oh my gosh, he’s never going to sleep. He’s always going to be a bad sleeper.’ And I just had to learn that a good day today doesn’t necessarily mean a good day tomorrow. A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

Dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. And all of those are really good reasons to ask for help.

Chloe: I didn’t know what I didn’t know. It was almost like I didn’t want to think about postpartum too much, because I truly didn’t know what to expect. Everyone talks about how it’s just such a big transition, and I did really feel that. What’s that thing that people say? Two people are born that day. The baby is born, but then you are also born as a mother. And I absolutely experienced that. You can try to prepare mentally for what it’s going to feel like, but it’s still so surreal when it actually happens.

Dr. Chambers: I immediately threw up my hands in thanks, and then I looked around like, ‘Wait a second.’ Everything is different. I felt like I didn’t even know which way to move or walk. I didn’t know what to do next. I just sat with that moment. My beliefs, my vision for tomorrow, my to-do list, it all just exploded, all in that moment. And it was immense joy, but a nervousness that I think is in proportion to just the depth and caliber of what this is.

Dr. Chambers: As someone who spent so long not being a mother, I never thought that motherhood would ever fully define me, and I still don’t feel that way today. I also think when you desire something so much, it’s hard sometimes to verbalize that desire. So knowing that you’re stepping into this role, this space, that has never really been in your control to step into, but that door is opening. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. Once I got that MD, I was going to be a doctor. But this is almost like it’s not an earned thing. It is given. I knew it was a forever shift, but spending so much time desiring to be in that role, and seeing that for myself and not knowing if it was going to happen, that was a real identity shift for me.

Chloe: I think a lot of the decisions I was making were just about being so much more cognizant of my own health. Before pregnancy, I don’t know if I was necessarily the healthiest person, but you get pregnant and suddenly it’s not about you, it’s about you and your baby. And your health is intertwined obviously. So it was just a lot of decisions about, you know, obviously I’m going to follow all the advice. I’m going to limit my caffeine intake and I’m going to avoid foods that could give me listeria. And I’m going to, you know, take my prenatal. All of a sudden I was thinking about my health so much more, in a way I hadn’t been before.

Dr. Chambers: So many of the decisions that I knew I had to make, it was almost like I had the answers to the test, just because I’m an OBGYN. But then I started to realize that what I really knew about pregnancy was related to a role that I wasn’t playing this time. I was the actual patient. I had a point in my pregnancy where my cervix was shorter, and they were measuring it, and wondering, are we going to need to do something more invasive, like a cerclage, or can we just do vaginal progesterone. And my very best friend, it was her bachelorette party, but it was in a remote area of Mexico, and I said, ‘How can I reconcile potentially delivering early in this extreme prematurity state that we would be looking at because I just want to be on this girls’ trip?’ I had to just sit with myself, ‘All right, what makes the most sense?’ Of course my friend was amazing and was like, ‘Girl, say less. No one’s going to feel bad. Take care of you and your baby.’ But it just was hard. You want to do so many things, but at the end of the day, you have to stand in your values and stand in your truths and trust that the people around you will be supportive of that.

Dr. Chambers: This day and age, it is just hard, but it depends on the topic. When I was making my registry, for whatever reason, I just couldn’t start it. There’s a billion strollers. What do you mean there’s this many cribs? I was so overwhelmed. So I gave my sister my login and said, ‘Go to town.’ But as it related to my health, being someone who had a high-risk pregnancy, it was a meeting of the minds. I made sure all of my doctors were on the same page, and I wanted a yes. Like when you’re in the emergency row of the flight and they’re like, ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ ‘Nephrologist?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘High-risk doctor?’ ‘Yes.’ OBGYN who’s doing the delivery, yes. I trusted my team.

Chloe: I was also overwhelmed by the whole registry process. But I don’t have a lot of friends who have been pregnant before me, so I was leaning on the internet a lot. Dr. Google, and honestly lots of YouTube videos, all those videos of people being like, ‘This is what’s on my registry,’ or ‘Day in the life.’ And then my OBGYN was so helpful. I would be lost without her. She was truly such a resource, and I really felt like I had built a trust with her, and it really paid off later during birth and everything. I felt like I could ask her anything and trusted her advice.

Dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

Dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s important to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

Dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s important to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. She recommended I get ABRYSVO for it, and I remain very happy that I listened to my OBGYN’s recommendation to get ABRYSVO when I was pregnant, and that helped protect him during his first six months of life when he is so vulnerable.

ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components. An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Chloe: I’m glad we’re talking about this, because sometimes it can feel like so many things are being thrown at you when you’re pregnant, especially if you don’t have a lot of knowledge going into it and then you’re hearing about things from your OBGYN. It can feel sort of rushed, where if I’m hearing about a vaccine in my 32-week appointment, but then they’re like, ‘Oh, by the way, you only have until your 36 weeks to get it.’ So the more you know going in, it can only help to be more informed, to have time to do research.

Dr. Chambers: The mental shift that was required the most, that I still carry with myself today, is letting go of the whole independent aspect. I would pride myself in being someone who was very self-sufficient. ‘I got it. If you can’t do this, I’ll figure it out.’ And it’s not that I don’t believe in myself, it is that I fully acknowledge the weight of motherhood and all that is required, and I now welcome the help. I had to tell my older sister, ‘I need you to put together my pump,’ and she did. I had to tell my mother-in-law, ‘The only thing I need today is a nap.’ And she’s like, ‘Go nap.’ Until you learn to verbalize those things and truly believe that you’re worthy of it, not as a point of insufficiency, motherhood requires a village. It requires a team. It requires support. Your mental health will be that much better for it.

Chloe: You go from being an individual with all of your independence, and then suddenly you are putting this baby’s needs before your own. My advice would be to try to establish communication with your village early, whoever that is, and have some sort of plan. Learn how to delegate. I don’t think I had done a lot of delegating before becoming a mom, and then suddenly you’re delegating all the time.

Chloe: I want him to see me as competent and capable, but I also want him to see me as playful and fun. I think that’s been a big part of it. Maybe especially having a little boy, I want to be playful with him, and I want him to be able to have that kind of relationship with me. The nurturing comes so easy, but the playfulness has come a little harder. I hope he looks back and he’s like, ‘You know what? We had fun.’

Dr. Chambers: I hope my son sees me as someone he can trust, as someone who can give him advice, as someone who always makes decisions that are grounded in love and goodness, and someone who’s been making decisions since before he was born to set him up to have the best possible life. I hope that he trusts me with every aspect of who he is, knowing that the love I have is profoundly unconditional, and it has been before I could even picture his face. Before I even knew who he was, he was always worthy of that love and support, and it’s not going anywhere.

This article has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the full episode of The Motherly Podcast on YouTube.

Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

You are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visit http://www.vaers.hhs.gov or call 1-800-822-7967.

Individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO at pfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

#7992. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

#7991. So You Think You Have Insomnia. What Now?

Even if you’re not comfortable taking medication, there are other treatment options out there.

When you’re a parent, it’s sometimes hard to tell what is a normal amount of tired and what’s an unhealthy level of exhaustion. Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings, it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep, there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers, board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

“If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” says Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

“Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up too early, or just having really poor, unrefreshing sleep. There are no guidelines on how long it takes you to fall asleep or how long you’re awake in the middle of the night, but you have to be unhappy with it at least three times a week for at least three months for it to meet full criteria for chronic insomnia,” Meers explains.

If you’ve noticed your husband starts snoring within seconds of his head hitting the pillow, you’re not alone. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which experts have chalked up to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the bulk of the mental load in the family.

“One of the biggest reasons we think for this is that as women, we cycle through our monthly menstrual cycle, and the dynamics and the changing of those hormones set us up to have more disrupted and more fragmented sleep at certain times of the cycle versus other times,” says Meers.

“Also, we have a lot of role strain as women. We carry a lot of caretaking activities and responsibilities, especially in women who are in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, who are trying to take care of everyone and have a career and be productive and make sure that we’re taking care of our kids the way we value or give them the life we want them to live. Stress directly impacts insomnia and our ability to sleep. So it really becomes this negative feedback cycle.”

You could definitely start by scheduling an appointment with your primary care doctor, if you have one. However, surveys show the average doctor only receives about 2.5 hours of education on sleep during medical school. Depending on your concerns and potential causes of your sleeplessness, they might refer you to a sleep medicine physician, a neurologist, a psychiatrist, or a sleep psychologist.

You may have never heard of sleep psychologists like Meers before, but they are specifically trained in the dynamics of sleep and sussing out underlying medical causes of insomnia (like sleep apnea) versus behavioral causes.

“I talk to a lot of primary care physicians. A lot of times they feel constrained to just give medications, nor do they have the time to really assess what’s going on because they have just so much to do in such a short amount of time,” Meers says. “So if you have the ability to see a sleep specialist like me who's a psychologist, I recommend starting there. And then if this is a medical issue, we are really good at determining that and then sending you along to the right treatment provider.”

Sleep psychologists are a great resource if you want to try other treatment options before turning to medication. The American Psychological Association has a psychologist finder where you can enter your zip code and search specifically for sleep psychologists in your area. You could also check with your insurance provider or ask your PCP if they know of any sleep psychologists near you.

Many people start trying to fix their sleep with supplements like melatonin or magnesium. They might turn to their primary care doctor next and either try a medication and love the results, or feel a little stuck because they don’t want meds, but there’s not much else being offered.

If there is an underlying medical cause for your sleeplessness, like restless legs syndrome or sleep apnea, treating that condition should alleviate the insomnia. For everyone else, Meers says medication can be a wonderful tool, but treatment should start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I.

“That’s what the research shows is most effective. So when somebody comes to me, I’m like, ‘I want you to do what’s going to be most effective for you.’ And so my goal is to start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia.”

CBT-I is very different from cognitive behavioral therapy to treat something like anxiety or depression. It helps bridge the connection between your biology and your psychology, Meers says.

“The way that cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia works is that we are using our understanding of the biology of sleep to get your behaviors in line with your biology. We are not just focusing on sleep timing, but also how your body has learned to sleep poorly and how do we unlearn that.”

CBT-I is actually a pretty short treatment, compared to most plans in the field of psychology — an average of just four to eight sessions, says Meers.

“It’s very skills-based, meaning I’m teaching a lot of skills in the first four sessions, and then for the next few sessions, we’re just tracking our progress and seeing how things are working. You are changing a lot of your habits, and you’re changing those habits in the service of retraining your body and your mind to associate the bed with sleep. I’m literally telling people to get out of bed, here’s what you do when you get out of bed, here’s what to think about, and then here’s when you get into bed, here’s your sleep schedule for the next week.”

The moral of the story is that you shouldn’t wait to tell someone — your PCP, a sleep psychologist, your usual therapist — about your sleep struggles. Whether you want to try CBT-I, find a medication that works for you, or investigate a possible issue like sleep apnea, there is help out there for sleeplessness.

#7989. 6 Plants That Need Mulching in November to Keep Roots Cozy as Temperatures Fall – and 4 You Should Never Cover

Protect vulnerable garden plants from winter cold with an insulating layer of mulch in late fall, but be selective or you could do more harm than good.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Late fall is an important time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the plan. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

Because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

Many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's important to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

If you’ve planted new perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

Mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

Many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

Reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

Your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see new growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

While many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your new garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

Always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

You can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

Coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

November is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s important to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

For all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

Winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

#7988. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

We spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.
