In terms of odor reduction, the Oneisall Air Purifier really makes a difference as part of my 3-pronged attack against stinky litter boxes:

Premium diet and good hydration to reduce odors at their source.

Optimal air purifier and litter box juxtaposition.

Maximized litter box hygiene and odor-trapping with an automatic litter box.

The only thing I hate about having a self-cleaning litter box is thinking about all the years I didnât have a self-cleaning litter box. So much time spent scooping and sifting. Resenting my catsâ every urination and bowel movement.

These days, instead of five litter boxes that needed daily attention, I have two Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Boxes. Once or twice a week, I empty the waste drawer, replace the waste bag, top up the litter, and give everything a brush or wipe. Once a month, I do a more thorough cleaning, which takes no longer than cleaning a regular litter box.

Before upgrading, my cats had several large, top-entry litter boxes. Like many cat parents, I had (selfishly) opted for enclosed litter boxes because they meant reduced odors and less litter spillage. Why selfish? Because the uncomfortable truth is that enclosed litter boxes are designed for human comfort, not feline preference.

It was immediately apparent when I introduced the open-top self-cleaning litter box from Oneisall that all my cats preferred to âpoo with a viewâ.

Cats are at their most vulnerable when toileting, and, unlike us, prefer to have a clear view of the world when they do their business. In multi-cat households, itâs not uncommon for cats to ambush each other as they exit a closed-in litter box. Sometimes itâs playful, sometimes itâs opportunistic bullying. Either way, it can make skittish felines even more reluctant to use the provided privy and potentially opt for an alternative location of their choosing.

The other issue is that while we enjoy the benefits of any overpowering odors being trapped inside an enclosed box, our cats are forced to breathe in all the aerosolized fecal matter and toxic ammonia gas every time they go to the toilet. Just because they produce it doesnât mean they want to inhale it.

With the Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Box, waste is locked away, along with the smell. I did empty the waste drawer more frequently over summer as the hot weather naturally increases the amount of ammonia in the air, which is to be expected.

Have I noticed an increase in the amount of cat litter on my floor? Yes, a bit. Although the litter trapping mats provided do help reduce litter tracking, I am definitely vacuuming more litter than I did in the past. And do I care? Heck no.

A bit of extra vacuum cleaning is a small price to pay for happier cats that are guaranteed to be met with a fresh litter tray for every visit.

For those who really hate the idea of a bit more litter on the ground, you can purchase an alternative litter guard from the Oneisall website for using pellet-type substrates, like tofu litter, which tends to track less.

The trouble with most product reviews is that they are rarely performed over a long enough period of time for any major issues to appear. After spending almost a year with my cat room kitted out with Oneisall products, I can honestly say that there are just three things I would change if I could:

Itâs petty and unimportant, but it still bothers me that the control unit is a creamy off-white, while almost everything else in the product range is either black, grey, or white. Just, why?

A fantastic and super important feature of the Oneisall Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Box is the various motion sensors, which prevent the cleaning cycle from starting if there is a cat in or near the box, and pause the cycle if the sensors detect motion nearby. I have found that, compared to some others, the sensors on this unit are particularly sensitive. They react when I walk past the door, and I have had the occasional tantrum when one of the sensors was detecting debris or imbalance or maybe a ghost. Overall, an overabundance of caution is always better than not enough, particularly when it comes to the safety of our pets, and though I am loathe to accuse anyone or anything of being too sensitive, I think they could probably benefit from a little bit of tweaking.

The waste drawer under the self-cleaning litter box comes out the side of the unit, something I just thought of as mildly irritating until I recently tried out a similar (but much smaller) unit with a front-opening waste drawer. This might seem like a minor problem, but depending on the location and positioning of your litter box, it does mean needing to shuffle and shimmy things around when it comes time to empty the drawer.

It did take me an embarrassingly long time to realize that the drawer can be inserted on either side, which makes it a bit easier, but if youâre short on space, a front-opening drawer would be better. A minor complaint but worth mentioning.

For the best product range and customer service experience, head to the Oneisall website. You can also find Oneisall products online and in-store from reputable retailers like Amazon, Chewy, PetSmart, Target, and Walmart.

Iâm sure some super-skittish scaredy-cats might be horrified the first time they witness their litter box rotating, and mine were certainly curious at first. Within 24 hours, these technological wonders had been accepted as just âpart of the furnitureâ. When I first introduced the automatic litter box, as recommended, I kept their old box available for the first week to give them time to adjust. Suffice it to say that with five cats, I only had to scoop the old litter box twice in that week.

Just the other day I watched Clutch walk up to the litter box whilst it was in the middle of a cleaning cycle, causing it to pause. He jumped in to relieve himself, apparently unconcerned that the tray was sitting at about a 30o angle! Not only did this demonstrate the importance of the Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Boxâs safety features, but it also showed how unbothered cats can be once something ânewâ becomes part of their everyday life.

All the products I have tried and tested from Oneisall are cleverly designed and have, so far, stood the test of time. Theyâre not the cheapest on the market, but they are most certainly not the most expensive, and considering the attention to detail and quality I have experienced firsthand, I think Oneisall is excellent value for money.

Absolutely! In fact, I recently bought myself a second Oneisall Air Purifier so I could have one upstairs and downstairs.

Itâs always difficult to cut through the noise of ads, reels, product reviews, and sponsored content to work out what to buy. Even with a Trustpilot score as impressive as Oneisallâs, you can never be sure how long people have been using a product before they post a review, which is why I wanted to take the opportunity to revisit this wonderful brand.

When it comes to kitting out my cat room, I donât just want the cheapest stuff, but I also donât like spending a fortune on designer brands or unnecessary bells and whistles. What I like about Oneisall is that their designs put the needs and comfort of pets first, with user-friendly products that are practical and affordable.

One year on, Iâm glad I discovered Oneisall, and more importantly, so are my cats.

#7887. Getting Answers from ER DVM Courtney Deer

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

If youâve seen The Pitt, youâve got an idea of what happens behind the scenes in an emergency vet hospital. Thereâs always another case to see, another owner to talk to, another patient to check up on. The biggest difference is that we donât often refer things. The initial emergency clinician is also the one assessing the radiographs, interpreting bloodwork, performing surgeries, and managing hospitalized cases. Itâs not uncommon for me to have a critical ICU patient Iâm managing at the same time as Iâm working up an ear infection, or about to go into surgery for a C-section.

Anyone who walks through the ER doors gets triaged, and I see what I can. This can be ear infections, severe dog bite wounds, or behavioral issues.

The most rewarding part of working in emergency veterinary medicine? When the patient is feeling good enough to try to bite you!

Initially, I wasnât sure if I wanted to go to veterinary school. I worked in a boarding clinic attached to a general practice that occasionally let me help on the medicine side, but I wasnât sold on vet med. I didnât get into veterinary school my first application round, so I found a job at a local emergency clinic. My working interview was so wild, I realized Iâd found my passion!

Emergencies come in waves! Some days are âDiarrhea Day,â where everything that comes in has diarrhea. I had âUrine Dayâ last week! By far, Iâd say GI upsets (vomiting, diarrhea, not eating) are the most common ER cases.

Seizures, protracted vomiting, severe weakness. I think anything that comes on suddenly should be investigated quickly!

If youâre worried, Iâm worried. You know your pet best, and if you feel something is âoffâ â donât wait! Even if itâs just for an exam or to get vitals, itâs well worth the peace of mind.

Itâs totally okay to be open about your budget and what you can and cannot do. The ER tends to be more expensive than a daytime practice, and we acknowledge that.  Our job is not to judge; itâs to help! If that means stabilizing until your vet can see you in a few hours, letâs do that.

I saw a lot of disinformation online. I figured if I was louder, I could drown out the bad advice.

I try to time my posts with real-world presentations. Heat stroke cases in the summer, toxicities around the holidays. Sometimes I just have a really interesting case, and I share it right then and there.

That veterinarians are humans too! I post a lot of information for other veterinary professionals, and I hope pet owners see the comments and realize how engaged the community is. Here is a group of people talking about vet med on their day off, learning about cases and new studies, and trying to keep up to date on the latest medicine.

Veterinary medicine is very science-focused. While we are always learning, thereâs a sort of structure to it that doesnât allow for much movement. My books are a whole different part of my brain, one where I can be creative and silly and make up worlds!

âAnother Damn Rescueâ is a spicy shifter romcom where a veterinarian finds an injured âdogâ on the side of the road, only to realize heâs a wolf shifter. Itâs ultimately a love letter to vet med, where I talk about the struggles we face, while also showing the humor and humanity. Oh, and how amazing veterinary technicians, assistants, and receptionists are!

Itâs more of a good time, kick your feet up and giggle sort of story! Pet owners might gain some insight into what itâs like to work in vet med in 2026. Veterinary professionals will enjoy seeing themselves accurately represented in media with a happy ever after!

The podcast is an extension of my social media â itâs a resource for other vets when theyâre not sure where to go. Itâs mostly focused on education for other veterinarians. I bring on specialists and let them pick a topic they feel passionate about. Think of it as continuing education.

Bridging my author identity with my veterinary one is very scary, but also very cool! Iâm especially excited about the podcast because I hope to get companies to talk about new products before they launch as well.

Fatigue! Thereâs compassion and ethical fatigue, where we feel helpless in the face of obstacles outside our reach. Some days I think, âI didnât help anyone today.â And thatâs not true; itâs the story we tell ourselves when weâre in that headspace.

Sometimes we need to take a step back and remember that this is that person's worst day. Ultimately, the team is there to help you. While we donât tolerate abuse, we TOTALLY UNDERSTAND being upset, overwhelmed, having decision paralysis, and everything else that goes along with these scary situations!

I am a pet owner as well as a veterinarian, and Iâve had cases that hit me as a pet owner as well. âIâve been in your shoes before,â goes a long way for owners in these situations. Weâre often told not to interject our opinions, but I am quick to tell owners that Iâve had a pet in the same situation.

Keep ALL of your records! Ask your vet to email you bloodworkand keep it in a folder. Take pictures of your pet's medications. Walking into the ER and saying âHereâs Fluffyâs last bloodworkâ and âhereâs the medication Fluffy is onâ is SO valuable!

XYLITOL!! It can cause fatal low blood sugar and liver damage. Itâs in sugar-free gum, and lately theyâve been calling it âbirch sugar,â so not a lot of people realize itâs the same thing.

Good mentorship is worth its weight in gold! Even the best veterinary school on the planet will not prepare you to step right into an ER without assistance. Ask for help, and find people who are willing to help you learn.

You can find Dr Courtney Deer on Instagram: @er.dvm.

Dr. Courtney Deer is an emergency veterinarian in Phoenix, AZ. She graduated from Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine in 2015, followed by a one-year rotating internship focused on emergency and critical care. She has worked exclusively in emergency medicine since completing her internship. Outside the ER, she is the creator of ER.DVM, a veterinary education platform focused on practical, evidence-based medicine, and the host of the 2 AM Consult podcast, where she interviews veterinary specialists about the cases and questions clinicians face in everyday practice.

After dazzling us with their fiery fall foliage, Japanese maples deserve a little TLC to help them weather winter and return in all their glory next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

Don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

However, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

Tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

In these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

If your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

Would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces new growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

In spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

You’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

This means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7885. Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago.  The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument.  The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film.  From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

But there is another important aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

The animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics.  Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:

There is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition.  This is called autoloading.  This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those new to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

The film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark shows an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

The film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

Animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round.  The film's animation shows the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

The film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning.  Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things.  The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

It has been said that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's new film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

NEXT: Has the Supreme Court Undercut the Courts?

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

#7883. Two Ginger Brothers Became the First Documented Cases of Marfan Syndrome in Cats

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats come in all shapes and sizes. Some have legs that seem a little too long for their bodies, others have ears big enough to pick up satellite signals, and a few look like they haven't quite grown into themselves yet.

But when Gary and Shaggy were kittens, their disproportionately long limbs turned out to be more than an unusual-looking but perfectly charming physical trait. The two brothers would eventually become the first domestic cats confirmed to have Marfan syndrome through genetic testing; not exactly what any cat owner would expect when bringing home a pair of kittens.

As the cats grew, veterinarians identified abnormalities affecting their eyes and enlargement of the aorta, the major blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Researchers at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute for Animal Health worked with veterinary and genetic specialists to investigate what was going on.

Their long limbs were one clue. The eye abnormalities and enlarged aortas added two more. Slowly, the pieces of the puzzle began to fit together, pointing researchers toward Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder far better known in human medicine than in veterinary practice. Genetic testing confirmed the connection, uncovering what made these two brothers so unusual.

Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue, the body's natural support system. This tissue helps give structure and strength to the bones, ligaments, skin, eyes, and blood vessels. When something goes wrong with this system, the effects can show up in several different ways.

In humans, the condition often causes unusually long limbs and fingers, a tall, slender build, eye abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiovascular complications.

Abraham Lincoln was famously tall and lanky, which has led to speculation that he may have had Marfan syndrome. No one can say for sure, though. Turns out, even Honest Abe left a few medical mysteries behind!

For Olympic volleyball player Flo Hyman, long limbs gave her an edge on the court. However, her life was tragically cut short, dying at age 31 from cardiac complications from Marfan syndrome.

One of the genes involved in Marfan syndrome is called FBN1. It contains the instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that helps maintain the structure and function of connective tissues throughout the body.

When that gene doesn't work as it should, the effects can extend well beyond a person's or animal's appearance. As the gorgeous ginger duo, Gary and Shaggy, began showing signs similar to those seen in humans with Marfan syndrome, their veterinary team started to wonder if cats could also suffer from the same condition.

Genetic sequencing revealed that Gary and Shaggy both carried two altered copies of FBN1. In other words, they had inherited the mutation from both parents.

In humans, Marfan syndrome typically develops when a person inherits one disease-causing copy of the gene. Having two altered copies is exceptionally rare and can be associated with more severe disease.

So the brothers presented researchers with an interesting puzzle.

Their particular genetic variant didn't completely prevent the gene from functioning. Instead, it partially disrupted how the gene's instructions were processed, allowing some normal fibrillin-1 function to remain, which may explain why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying two copies of the variant.

Their genetic instructions weren't simply switched on or off; it was something in between, which may help explain why the brothers developed the way they did.

Genes rarely behave like a tidy set of instructions. The effects of a genetic change depend on the specific variant involved and how it affects the resulting protein. Sometimes, a seemingly insignificant variation can have catastrophic consequences, altering the way the body functions.

The case of Gary and Shaggy is undeniably rare, and Marfan syndrome is unlikely to find its way onto the list of common feline diseases. However, in diagnosing and documenting the condition, veterinarians have something they didn't have before: a confirmed case of feline Marfan syndrome to help recognize, investigate, and compare with future cases.

These findings may help veterinary teams identify similar cases and better understand how particular FBN1 variants affect cats. They also demonstrate the value of bringing clinicians, genetic researchers, and pet parents together when a case doesn't fit neatly into an existing diagnosis.

Gary and Shaggy's shared genetic variant offered researchers a valuable opportunity to investigate the relationship between their physical features and the underlying condition.

Their owner, Nicole Desmond, also contributed to this process, and Cornell has highlighted the case as an example of how pet parents can collaborate with veterinary and genetic experts to advance knowledge that may eventually benefit other animals.

Even more importantly, Nicole loved the unique feline brothers with her whole heart. Vets did not expect either cat to survive for long, but they defied the odds. Gary was 6 years old when he passed away in July 2024, and in November 2025, at the incredible age of 7, Shaggy joined his brother across the rainbow bridge.

And that's one of the interesting things about veterinary medicine. Not every discovery starts with a large clinical trial or a disease affecting thousands of patients. Sometimes, it begins with two unusual kittens and a veterinary team willing to keep asking questions.

The rarity of this case means we donât necessarily have to think the worst when we see a long-legged kitten; itâs far more likely that theyâre simply long-limbed and not harboring a rare genetic disorder. However, it reminds us to pay attention to the bigger picture, bring unusual findings to the veterinarian's attention, and not automatically assume that two seemingly unrelated problems have nothing to do with each other.

Sometimes, a strange-looking kitten is simply a strange-looking kitten.

And sometimes, those extra-long legs are the first clue to a genetic story that researchers have never documented in cats before.

Your garden beds may be looking tired, but there's no need for back-breaking work. Just four simple layers can help replenish them in time for spring planting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

So just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

This low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

You can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

When you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

Then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

This is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

You aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially important if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

The bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the new, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

If you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

If you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

#7880. Paws and Effect: The Reasons Behind a Cat’s Sudden Aggression

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

We all know that feline behavior can be somewhat unpredictable. Just when you think youâve got it all figured out, a cat is already three steps ahead of you. But thereâs a big difference between normal feline quirks and uncharacteristic aggression.

A cat that has always been gentle and suddenly starts lashing out may be reacting to something in its environment, changing hormones, pain, or a health problem. Aggression has many causes, from fear and frustration to competition with other cats. Understanding what has changed can help identify the cause and determine the best way to respond.

Unneutered male cats may fight over access to females, particularly when several cats are competing for mates in the same area. When a female cat is in heat, she may attract multiple males, making fights more likely.

Female cats can also behave differently during heat cycles. Many become unusually affectionate and demanding of attention, while others may become irritable or aggressive. Hormonal changes can also affect how they interact with other cats, particularly other females.

Spaying/neutering is an important aspect of taking care of a cat. Not only does it help to minimize aggression and friction between cats, but it also prevents unwanted litters and helps reduce the risk of certain diseases.

Pain can make even a normally friendly cat lash out. A cat may react aggressively if someone touches a sore area or approaches when it is feeling unwell.

Urinary tract disease can make a cat pretty miserable, and males in particular are vulnerable to urinary blockages, which are extremely painful and can become life-threatening. A cat that is straining to urinate or unable to pass urine needs emergency veterinary attention.

Infections, injuries, arthritis, and cancer are often painful but difficult to recognize from the outside. If aggression appears suddenly or seems linked to discomfort, a veterinary examination is an important first step.

A frightened cat may respond aggressively when startled, even if it is usually relaxed and friendly. A sudden noise, an unfamiliar person, or another threatening experience can trigger a defensive reaction.

Ongoing stress can also contribute to aggression. Cats that feel unsafe in their surroundings may remain on edge and react defensively to people or animals around them.

Every cat should have access to a quiet, comfortable place where it can retreat without being disturbed. Giving a frightened cat space can help it feel more secure.

Not every aggressive-looking interaction is driven by anger or fear. Play helps cats practise their hunting skills, and some become too rough when playing with people or other animals.

However, rough play should not be encouraged because biting and scratching can cause injuries. Rewarding gentle play and redirecting a cat toward appropriate toys can help it learn more acceptable ways to use its energy.

Cats can be protective of their territory, so the arrival of another animal may trigger aggression. The newcomer could be a new cat or dog in the household, or an outdoor cat that has started visiting the yard.

Sometimes, owners may not even realize another cat is nearby. Seeing or smelling an unfamiliar animal can leave a cat agitated, causing it to react to other pets or people.

Aggressive behavior plus inappropriate urination and scent-marking are not uncommon when a cat feels its territory is under threat.

A cat that becomes frustrated by something it cannot reach may take that frustration out on another target. This is known as redirected aggression.

For example, a cat might become agitated after seeing another cat outside, then lash out at a person or pet nearby. The target may have done nothing wrong and simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Giving an agitated cat time and space to calm down is safer than trying to handle it immediately.

Cats living together usually have established social relationships, and introducing a new pet tends to upset the status quo. A certain amount of fighting and posturing is to be expected as the cats adjust to the change, but escalating aggression or bullying of one cat should be addressed.

Introducing a new animal gradually can help reduce conflict. Cats should have time to become familiar with each other without being forced into close contact before they are ready.

Some cats seem to enjoy attention but suddenly bite or scratch once petting begins. A cat may become overstimulated by touch, or it may simply want to be near a person without being handled.

Watch for signs of discomfort, such as flattened ears or a flicking tail. If a cat seems agitated, stop petting and give it space. Treats can reward calm interactions when the cat is comfortable.

Aggression can be difficult for a household to manage, but many causes can be addressed with patience and the right approach. Rewarding calm behavior, avoiding known triggers, and providing a safe place to retreat can all help.

The first step is to work out why the cat is behaving differently. If the aggression is sudden, it may be linked to pain or illness, so you should always consult a veterinarian before treating it as a behavioral issue. Once medical causes are excluded, look for changes â both indoors and outside the home â that might be affecting your cat.

Simple steps like providing extra hiding places, calming aids, and adapting handling techniques can go a long way to reducing feline aggression.

#7877. 70+ Dogs Rescued From South Korean Meat Farm as 2027 Ban Approaches

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Nearly 30 dogs have arrived in New York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

A plane ride to New York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

On October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

For the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

And yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

When the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

It's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is currently hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

Humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

In this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

More than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to New York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

Rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

South Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

In May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

According to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

Itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. So, while the closure of dog meat farms is good news, itâs not a true victory if these dogs are simply moved on to face the same fate. The ban is a huge step forward, but a law is only as good as its enforcement.

The real goal isn't just to close the farms. It's making sure the dogs are actually safe.

Getting out of the farm is the first big hurdle for these dogs. Now comes veterinary care, recovery, and the not-so-small task of learning how to live in a completely different world.

Humane World for Animalsâ rescue protocols include veterinary exams, vaccinations, respiratory screening when needed, and the health documents required for international travel. Each dog has their own needs. Some may need treatment for skin problems, wounds, dental disease, or nutritional deficiencies.

The second, and perhaps most challenging, hurdle for these dogs is adapting to a whole new way of life. Just because a dog has been saved doesn't automatically mean a dog feels safe.

Imagine never having lived in a home, then suddenly finding yourself surrounded by doors, stairs, strange noises, slippery floors, and humans who keep trying to show you how much they love you. Even a well-meaning hug could be overwhelming. And the vacuum cleaner? Let's just say it probably won't be winning any popularity contests.

These dogs may need to learn things many pets take for granted: how to explore a room, relax around people, or understand that a hand reaching toward them isn't something to fear. Some will be curious from the start. Others may prefer to watch from a safe distance. Neither response is wrong, and patience plus a little common sense go a long way.

A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every new experience into a test.

Adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

Those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a new home environment.

The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. Some dogs adjust quickly, while others may take a little longer than 3 days. The important thing to know is that this version of the dog is not usually a good representation of their true selves.

Over the first 3 weeks, dogs will start to gain confidence and explore their new world. They are often testing boundaries, becoming familiar with patterns, and learning how to trust. Being consistent and providing predictable routines is paramount to this process.

By the time 3 months have passed, most dogs will be feeling more settled. It may still take some time for their full personality to appear, but with every passing month, they become more confident, more trusting, and less anxious.

Sometimes progress looks like taking a treat from someone's hand. Sometimes it's finally falling asleep without startling at every sound. Those moments might not make a flashy before-and-after video, but for that dog, they're a big deal.

One more thing: fear and behavioural changes shouldn't automatically be dismissed as consequences of a dog's past. Pain, illness, and other medical problems can affect behaviour, too. If a dog seems persistently distressed or suddenly starts acting differently, a veterinary check is important. We don't want to assume it's trauma when there may be pain due to a treatable medical issue behind it.

A second chance isn't just getting a dog out of a cage. It's giving them the medical care, space, and time to discover that life can be safe, and maybe even pretty wonderful.

Humane World for Animals calls the Gangjin operation its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea. But that doesn't mean the work is over. The organization plans to continue monitoring the ban and supporting efforts to enforce it.

Closing farms is a huge win. Full stop. But making sure dogs aren't left behind, moved elsewhere, or subjected to illegal practices is part of making that win count. With the ban taking full effect in February 2027, the coming months will be crucial.

For the dogs already rescued, a new life is finally within reach. Veterinary care. Rehabilitation. A chance to find a home where the biggest worry is whether they get the good spot on the sofa. That's quite the upgrade.

Now, we turn our attention to the dogs still waiting in South Koreaâs remaining farms. Stopping the dog meat trade is a huge victory, but in many ways, itâs just the beginning. Saving these dogs is more than just stopping the slaughter. Itâs making sure they all get the happy ending they deserve.

#7876. Fostering Is In My Blood

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

I remember when my mom brought home our first fosters. I was in fifth grade, and when my twin sister, Becca, and I came home from school, our mom walked us over to a box with three little neonatal kittens, just days old: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy. With closed eyes and little bodies running purely on instinct, they wriggled over one another, crying out to be fed. I watched as my mom gently picked them up, and as she did, she turned to us, smiling, and said, âtheyâre your responsibilityâ.

I was flooded with excitement and fear all at once. I knew nothing about caring for something so small. I watched in awe as my mom bottle-fed them one by one. The meowing subsided, and their little ears wiggled as they latched on and ate until their tiny bellies were full. The lesson had begun regardless of my fears. But feeding, I quickly learned, was just step one.

Soon after, we were stimulating each kitten to go potty, testing the temperature of their enclosure, wiping them clean, and getting them settled in for a post-bottle nap. So much happened so quickly, and they were so small and fragile. I told my mom I was nervous that I wouldnât be able to do what she did. She laughed and, with a grin, informed me I would have plenty of time to learn: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy would need to eat every 2 hours, even throughout the night. So we had lots of chances to practice and retain all the new skills she was showing us.

Over the next few weeks, we watched them grow and grow until they were ready to find their forever homes. As adoption day approached, it was incredibly hard. My sister and I begged our mom to let us keep the kittens. After all, we had raised them, and our love for them was undeniable. But she assured us that this was a good thing; letting them go meant we could help more animals in need. In the moment, however, I didnât understand. Instead, I cried myself to sleep holding the kittens. My kittens.

Then the day came, and even though the adopters were my friends, I bristled when they knocked at the door. But as they came in and met Amelia, Angel and Buddy, something magical happened: I watched my friends fall in love with them just like I had. They giggled at the clumsy way Buddy walked. Their hearts melted as they watched the girls cuddle in the sun. I was still scared to let the kittens go, but now part of me was excited, too. My friends saw them how I saw them. I had to trust that the little babies that we raised were on to bigger and better things. Things that would allow us to welcome another baby in need. But still, my heart broke - I had fallen in love with each of them, and saying goodbye terrified me.

There wasnât much time after they were adopted to worry about my fears, though. Before I knew it, we said hello to our next foster: a skittish and energetic 5-week-old boy we called Kipper. I thought maybe this time Iâd try to guard my heart, but Kipper stole it anyway. His silly antics and never-ending supply of energy made it impossible not to fall in love with him, too. Part of me hoped that maybe this time, Kipper could stay. But my mom held firm, and a few weeks later another friend came to us to adopt. I watched it play out all over again. I smiled as they swooned over this little precious kitten and all his quirks, just like I had.

This time, though I was still heartbroken, I felt a sense of understanding settle in, too. I remember thinking to myself, as Kipper fell asleep, purring, in my friendâs arms, âI wonder who we will get to help next?â

It didnât take long for that question to get its answer: Four tiny black-and-white kittens found in a hot tub and brought to our doorstep. Three were friendly; one, wellâ¦he was anything but! Cleo, Leo, and Brandy settled in beautifully, but Bindy just needed more.

More time, more attention, more understanding.

I felt drawn to him, and while my twin tended to the others, I found myself focused on Bindy. He would hide, hiss, spit, and bite. But really, he was just a little thing in a big world, and he was terrified. I worked with him every day, and slowly but surely, he made progress. When adoption day came around, however, we decided Bindy wasnât ready yet. He stayed behind to gain more confidence and, in time, became our first foster-fail.

Sometimes it was best for a foster to be adopted, but sometimes, they were already home.

Bindy eventually became the most loving cat I ever knew. He was my soul cat, and my best friend. And even though he stayed, I didnât avoid the heartbreak that came with saying goodbye; it just came many, many years later when old age finally took him. I learned a second lesson from Bindy then: there is no love without loss and, despite the pain, love would always be worth it.

So I continued to dive in, foster after foster. Heartbreak after heartbreak. Miracle after miracle. And it was always worth it; just like my mom said it would be. Iâm no longer the little girl learning from my mother; those lessons are now a part of me. Theyâre one of the things she left behind after a lifetime of love. My heart broke saying goodbye to her, too, but her teachings gave me a life thatâs filled to the brim with purpose. And paired with a passion inspired by my first foster fail, Bindy, I quickly developed a soft spot for the âspicyâ foster cats; and thatâs what I do now.

Currently, a euthanasia-list survivor is calling my home their safe haven. Just like Bindy, Simon wasterrified and aggressive, and he almost paid for it with his life. While Iâve been fostering him, however, Iâve gotten to know a completely different cat than the one in the shelter. A cat thatâs full of love and silly antics, whoâs eager to hold a conversation and meow for your attention. A cat who just needed a chance.

When his adoption day comes, I know my heart will break again; it always does. Itâs the price we pay for loving something, and Iâll pay that price over and over again because it means I get to watch someone adore him in all the ways I have, and more. The internet will go into an uproar demanding I keep him, but my momâs voice will sound clearly in my ear and keep me grounded:

âItâs a good thing. Letting them go means we can help others in need.â

So I'll say goodbye, knowing another Simon, Bindy, or Kipper is waiting for their chance to be loved. And as I walk back into the shelter, the lesson I began learning all those years ago in fifth grade remains true: Fostering Saves Lives.

As a third-generation animal rescuer, Rachael Rae Robertson has truly never had a moment where her life didnât revolve around animals â and she wouldnât have it any other way. Her grandmother had a farm for retired racetrack horses and farm animals, her aunt worked in wildlife rehabilitation, and her mom focused on pets like bunnies, dogs, birds, and cats. Though all three of these inspirational women are no longer here with us, their lessons remain. Now, Rachael hopes to share the gifts they gave her and her twin sister, Becca, with the world. She hopes to inspire others to dip their toes into the world of rescue, too, whether itâs through fostering, volunteering, or activism. In her free time, she can be found in her happy place â aka with her tetrad of tabbies and senior pup!

Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling’s Christmas tree display is ever so chic, and ever so easy to make yourself using cuttings from your own garden...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private. So sue us, then, that we get excited when they offer us a sneak-peek into their world... especially when it comes with a Christmassy twist!

Now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity. Honestly, though, most stars seem to be taking a laidback approach to their festive decor of late, whether it's the Beckhams' bow-filled Christmas tree, Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, or even Michelle Obama's twig tree.

Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees. Check it out:

And just like that, they've proven you don’t need a large traditional evergreen tree to make your house look stylish during the holidays. In fact, if you decide to follow in Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's footsteps, you might not need to buy much at all.

All you have to do is take a simple stroll around your garden with a pair of pruners and a small pot to get the same look; fortunately, some experts told me exactly how to do it.

“The best mini Christmas trees start with a walk around your own garden,” says Nick Alan, founder of Palma Botanical Co., who has been growing plants for 25 years.

His picks? “Conifer tips like cedar, cypress, juniper and fir hold their needles longest. Boxwood and rosemary fill gaps and add scent.”

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

For clean cuts, Nick Alan recommends these Fiskars SoftGrip bypass pruners.

Use gentle hands with the shrub, though. “Harvest on a cool morning with clean pruners, cutting just above a side shoot so the plant regrows, and take no more than a third of any shrub,” says Alan.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a simple pot method for getting the Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling look this Christmas.

“Fill a 4-inch pot with damp sand (this will help hold your stems upright and will allow you to leave the tree in its pot as it dries). Remove the needles from the bottom 2 inches of each stem (you don’t want any foliage to rot in the sand!).”

Once this is done, she says you should “arrange the stems from tallest in the middle to shortest as you work your way out (creating a cone shape).” Remember, though, that cut foliage won’t last forever. “Mist every few days and keep it away from the stove, dishwasher vent, and sunny windows. Expect two to three weeks, swapping tired sprigs,” says Alan.

A living tree means you don’t have the extra work of worrying about sprigs. “For a kitchen island display like Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's, I like a living miniature tree best, because it does two jobs at once: it looks festive, and it stays useful after Christmas,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Brooks says rosemary is the practical pick for a kitchen: “Rosemary is the most practical in a kitchen because you can pick sprigs for cooking, and it smells wonderful near the stove.”

For care, Brooks says: “I keep young trees in cool spots away from radiators and water the compost so it stays lightly damp but never wet.” Alan adds: “Give it your brightest window, water when the top inch is dry, and plant it out afterward in zone 8 and warmer.”

Your kitchen island may be a great spot for trees, but don’t forget it’s also a workspace for cooking. Keep your trees all to one side and never let them near heat sources, especially the dry foliage.

Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says that “a little greenery with one beautiful ribbon often looks more considered than a crowded arrangement.”

For the layout, Melam says: “I love displaying mini trees in odd-numbered clusters of varying heights. Negative space is key! I’d keep the tallest stem 10-12 inches so as not to compete with faucets, etc.”

A tray helps too: “Displaying them on a tray or wooden slab can help tie them together & unify the display (as opposed to them looking like random pots on a counter).” On a budget, Alan says: “Pine cones, dried orange slices and ribbon dress them cheaply.”

Alan has one note of advice for people with pets or small children: “Skip holly, yew and mistletoe around pets and kids, since all are toxic.”

While Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling have both played a variety of characters throughout their film careers, we really do think that “people with a stunning Christmas kitchen island” is one we really fancy having a go at, too.

#7874. Five High-Tech Products That Understand Your Cat’s Instinctual Needs

As a cat parent, youâll no doubt be aware that living with cats is a completely different game than owning other pets. But did you know that this isnât just a matter of perception?

Cats have only been domesticated for about half as long as dogs have. On top of that, their genes are much less susceptible to âshapingâ than those of dogs. The result? Cats have retained more wild feline physical traits, instincts, and tendencies than dogs.

Not only does this have a significant impact on feline behavior, but it also shapes how we care for them.

This fact has been the driving force behind Petlibro's approach to high-tech cat care products. From pet fountains and automatic feeders to self-cleaning litter boxes, this company understands cats and knows exactly what they need to stay healthy and happy.

Here, we take a closer look at five of their productsâeach designed for your catâs specific needs while making your life easier.

Cats are complex creatures, and it takes more than love, cuddles, and the occasional tasty treat to keep them truly engaged, enriched, and thriving. In fact, they often need more than what the average owner can provide with their own two hands.

I could go on all day about the importance of a high-quality diet for your cat. But today, I want to talk about an aspect of the feline diet most owners might not think about: the importance of small, consistent, proportioned meals.

Cats evolved as hunters of relatively small prey, so their natural feeding pattern is quite different from ours and from the typical pet dog.

A wild cat might spend much of its day moving through its territory, hunting, and eating multiple small meals when the opportunity presents itself. They are not accustomed to sitting down to one or two large meals each day.

Although the process of domestication means that your feline family member no longer needs to hunt down their next meal, those instincts haven't completely disappeared just because their food comes in a bowl.

Even more so than eating habits, drinking habits in cats are highly tied to their instincts and physiological needs.

Domestic cats evolved from desert wild cats. That arid climate impacted their relationship to water in two key ways:

First, desert wild cats evolved to get most of their water from their preyâwhich isnât much. This means their kidneys are highly specialized to retain water and pass very little of it through their urine. For a cat that eats several juicy mice each day, this is all well and good. For a pet cat eating dry food, the need to consume water is dramatically increased if they are to keep this super-efficient system running properly. However, the instinct to actively seek out drinking water has not entirely caught up with the domesticated catâs lifestyle.

This brings us to cat hydration key number two: Desert wild cats know better than to drink stagnant water. In hot, arid climates, still water breeds bacteria and other dangerous organisms. As a result, cats are naturally attracted to fresh, flowing water that is much safer to drink; something that remains true for our pets.

Your kitty may be a skilled hunter and the apex predator of your home, but, like their wildcat ancestors, they can also be prey animals, with instincts that evolved to evade larger predators. One place this becomes evident is in their bathroom habits.

Cats bury their urine and feces to hide the scent from potential predators and competitors, so a stinky litter box feels anything but safe. And if they donât feel safe there, they may find other places to eliminate waste. Or worse, hold it in, causing kidney and digestive issues.

These three key areas are where Petlibroâs products shine. Created with your catâs natural instincts and needs in mind, they were also designed to make your life easier.

Allowing pets to graze or âfree-feedâ is a major cause of obesity in domestic cats. Because their wild ancestors never knew when their next meal was coming, their instincts tell them to eat whenever food is available. If itâs always available, some cats will simply keep on eating, even if they donât feel hungry.

An automatic feeder does a lot more than make mealtime convenient. It can actually help you create a feeding routine that better suits your cat's instincts, providing several small meals throughout the day, rather than one or two large ones.

From a human perspective, an automatic feeder can also provide that âcrack of dawnâ meal many cats crave, without you having to leave the comfort of your bed!

Petlibro offers several levels of smart feeding, depending on how much insight and personalization you want.

PETLIBRO 5G WiFi Automatic Pet Feeder: With customizable feeding schedules and precise portion control, the Petlibro 5G Automatic Feeder takes the guesswork out of consistent meals. Manage your cat's feeding routine remotely with WiFi, and create personalized meal calls that let them know when it's time to eat.

PETLIBRO RFID WiFi App Controlled Automatic Pet Feeder: In a multi-cat household, "mealtime" doesn't always mean every cat eats the same food at the same time. This feeder uses an RFID collar tag to give each pet exclusive access to its own food while tracking individual eating habits through the app. That makes it particularly useful for cats with different dietary needs or feeding patterns.

PETLIBRO Granary 2 Vision Smart Camera Feeder: For owners who want to understand their cat's eating habits, as well as manage them, this feeder adds a 1080p camera, motion detection, feeding logs, and smart notifications to scheduled, portion-controlled meals. You can even use personalized meal calls and two-way audio to stay connected when you're away.

These automatic pet feeders from Petlibro turn mealtimes into another way to understand your cat, helping you provide the consistency they need in a way that matches their instincts.

If your cat seems inexplicably fascinated by the faucet, they may actually be telling you something. Cats instinctively prefer fresh, moving water. By embracing the behavior that helped their wild ancestors survive, a water fountain can help our pets thrive.

The PETLIBRO Dockstream 2 Smart Cordless Fountain taps into that instinct while simultaneously helping you keep track of your cat's hydration.

Its pet-sensing mode activates the flow when your cat approaches, while a four-layer filtration system helps keep water fresh and clean. Just as important, the Petlibro App lets you monitor drinking habits and alerts you to changes in water intake, water levels, filter replacement, and cleaning.

With a cordless design and long battery life, you can give your cat the fresh, flowing water they instinctively seek without needing to keep the fountain tethered to an outlet, meaning you can place the fountain in whichever location your cat prefers.

A self-cleaning litter box isnât just about making our lives easier; itâs about providing your cat with a fresh litter box for every visit, without having to scoop multiple times a day. Cats need a space that is clean, private, and feels safe. That makes keeping the litter box tidy and odor-free an important part of supporting their natural behavior.

The PETLIBRO Luma Smart Automatic Cat Litter Box with Camera ensures a clean, safe bathroom space while turning the litter box into a source of useful information about your cat.

Luma automatically scoops after each visit, keeping the box consistently clean while locking away odors with a built-in carbon deodorizer. But the real high-tech advantage is what happens behind the scenes. The Lumaâs camera and AI software recognize up to ten individual cats and log their litter box visits, while waste analysis can help detect changes in urine and stool. You can even check in through the camera and receive alerts about unusual activity, including increased or decreased use.

In other words, Luma doesnât just help your cat establish a healthy bathroom routine, but it also gives you the data you need to see critical changes in health before they become something more.

The common thread among all of these products is simple: The best technology doesnât try to change what makes cats, cats. It works with them.

By understanding the instincts that still shape how our domesticated companions eat, drink, and eliminate, Petlibro turns everyday cat care into an opportunity to support those natural needs while giving owners more insight and peace of mind.
